n: Chapter 35 condemned Edom’s mountains; now Ezekiel speaks a message of hope to the mountains of Israel themselves. The land is addressed like a person who has suffered and will be comforted.

f.g: The Lord’s usual title for Ezekiel—a reminder that he is a mortal sent with God’s word.

n: Israel’s enemies gloated after Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, crowing that even Israel’s ancient hills now belonged to them. The Lord takes their taunt personally.

f.g: A cry of gloating at someone else’s misfortune.
Hilltops; here simply the high ground of the land, claimed as plunder.

n: The neighbors had stripped the land bare and turned Israel into a joke and a byword. To be “taken up in the lips of talkers” means to become the subject of gossip and mockery.

f.g: The remaining nations nearby—Edom, Ammon, Moab, Philistia.
Disgrace, bad reputation.

n: The Lord addresses every part of the land—hills, streams, valleys, ruined towns—as if calling each one by name. None of the devastated places is forgotten.

f.g: Scorn, ridicule.

n: God’s “jealousy” here is His protective zeal for His people and land. Edom (Idumea) especially rejoiced to seize Judah’s territory after the Babylonian conquest.

f.g: The Greek form of Edom, the nation descended from Esau.
Hebrew qinʾah—intense, protective zeal, not petty envy.

n: Israel has endured the shame heaped on it by the nations. The Lord now declares that He has heard and will act.

f.w: borne the shame of the heathen

n: Lifting the hand was a gesture of solemn oath. The Lord swears that the mockers will themselves experience the shame they poured on Israel.

f.w: I have lifted up mine hand
f.g: An oath gesture, like raising the hand to swear.

n: A turning point: the barren mountains will sprout and bear fruit again, because God’s people are about to come home. The land itself prepares for the return.

f.w: they are at hand to come
f.g: The return is near—fulfilled in part after Cyrus’s decree (538 BC) and, Latter-day Saints believe, more fully in the latter-day gathering.

n: “I am for you”—after years of judgment, God declares Himself on the land’s side. Fields that lay wild will be plowed and planted again.

f.g: The reverse of “I am against thee” spoken to Edom and others.

n: The whole house of Israel—not only Judah but all the tribes—will fill the land again, and ruined towns will be rebuilt.

f.w: all the house of Israel, even all of it

n: God promises not merely restoration but something better than Israel’s beginnings. The repeated refrain “ye shall know that I am the LORD” shows the goal: that people will come to know Him.

f.w: will do better unto you than at your beginnings
ye shall know that I am the LORD
f.g: Ezekiel’s signature phrase, used more than 60 times.

n: The land that once seemed to swallow its inhabitants through war and famine will become a safe inheritance where Israel’s children are no longer lost.

f.g: Leave them childless; take away their people.

n: Outsiders had said the land was cursed—a land that “eats” its people. The spies in Moses’ day had used almost the same words.
The Lord reverses that reputation. The land will no longer be known for death and loss.
Israel will no longer hear the taunts of the nations or stumble into the sins that brought its downfall.

f.g: Insult, disgrace.

n: A new message begins. Having promised to restore the land, the Lord now explains why Israel lost it and what He will do to change Israel’s heart.
Israel’s own behavior made the land ritually unclean. The comparison uses the Law of Moses’ language of ritual impurity to show how serious their sins had become.

f.g: A woman set apart during menstruation, considered ritually unclean under the Law of Moses.

n: Violence and idolatry were the two great sins that brought the exile. Innocent blood and false worship polluted the land God had given them.

f.w: the blood that they had shed

n: Scattering among the nations was the consequence Moses had warned of. God’s judgment matched their conduct.

f.w: I scattered them among the heathen

n: Even in exile, Israel dishonored God. The nations sneered, “These are supposed to be the Lord’s people, yet they were thrown out of His land”—making God look weak or unfaithful.

f.g: Brought disrespect on God’s reputation.

n: The Lord’s concern is for His “name”—His character and reputation among all peoples. His mercy flows from who He is.
Israel’s restoration will not be a reward for their goodness; it flows from God’s own faithfulness and holiness. This is grace: undeserved help given for His name’s sake.
When God restores and transforms His people, the nations will see His holiness displayed in them. A changed people becomes the evidence of a living God.

f.w: I shall be sanctified in you
f.g: God’s holiness will be shown openly through what He does in Israel.

n: The gathering: God will bring Israel out of every land back to its own. Latter-day Saints see both the ancient return and the modern gathering of Israel in this promise.

f.w: gather you out of all countries
f.r: Ezekiel 37:21; Isaiah 11:11-12; 3 Nephi 20:29; Articles of Faith 1:10

n: Sprinkled water was used in the Law of Moses for purification. Here it pictures God Himself washing away sin and idolatry; many Christians see an image of baptism and spiritual cleansing.

One of the great promises of the Old Testament: God will replace a hard, unresponsive “heart of stone” with a living, feeling “heart of flesh.” True change comes from the inside, and God is the one who brings it about.

f.w: A new heart also will I give you

f.g: A heart that is hard, cold, and unable to respond to God.

n: God’s own Spirit will dwell in them and empower them to obey. Obedience becomes the fruit of a changed heart, not a burden imposed from outside.

f.w: I will put my spirit within you

n: The covenant formula—“ye shall be my people, and I will be your God”—sums up the relationship God has always wanted with Israel.

f.w: ye shall be my people, and I will be your God

n: The Lord promises both spiritual and physical blessings: cleansing from sin and abundant grain with no famine. “Corn” in the KJV means grain in general, not maize.

f.g: Grain such as wheat or barley.

n: Fruitful trees and fields will end the shame of famine that made Israel a laughingstock. God’s blessing on the land will be visible to everyone.
Grace leads to genuine repentance. When Israel sees how good God has been, they will look back on their sins with honest sorrow and disgust.

f.g: Loathe—feel deep shame and revulsion at your own past behavior.

n: The Lord repeats that He acts for His name’s sake, not because Israel earned it. Humility is the right response to unearned mercy.

f.g: Embarrassed, put to shame.

n: Cleansing comes first, then rebuilding. Spiritual renewal precedes the restoration of cities and homes.
Travelers who once passed a wasteland will see cultivated fields. The change will be obvious to everyone.
People will compare the restored land to the garden of Eden—a picture of paradise regained. The ruined cities will be fortified and full of people again.

f.g: Fortified with walls.

n: The restoration will prove to the surrounding nations that Israel’s God keeps His word. “I the LORD have spoken it, and I will do it” is a guarantee.

f.w: I the LORD have spoken it, and I will do it

n: Though God has promised all this, He still invites Israel to ask Him for it. Prayer is part of how His promises are fulfilled.

f.w: I will yet for this be inquired of

n: At Jerusalem’s great festivals, the city overflowed with flocks of sacrificial animals. In the same way, the empty cities will overflow with people.

f.g: The appointed holy festivals such as Passover and Tabernacles.
